items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: They went on the Cavett show... on Cavett, because Cavett was always — you know he was a very verbal guy, so he put musicians on a panel and talked to them

ctx.x: I see. Do you think those musicians who were playing, I mean Archie Schepp’s music, just to use his name with that genre, this is music that’s let’s say challenging for the average listener. Do you think that they honestly thought that if they got the right amount of exposure in magazines and the media that they could sell more records?

Yes, absolutely. I mean Archie, who is a very clever fellow and very sophisticated, was perfectly aware that doing things, writing, expressing himself verbally and doing things that were to some extent deliberately provocative, that that should result in people wanting to check out his music and also that he might enlist people who were politically on the same wavelength and so on. Yes, absolutely. And it must be said that the avante © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

garde in jazz was very publicity-conscious. They were very much aware of the fact that if they were making provocative statements and all these things — and the music itself of course was aggressive, some of it. Interestingly enough, I mean Ornette’s music was never — Ornette very rarely, although he sometimes said things — he usually had to do with recognition of his music rather than putting it on a more universal social-political platform.
